extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and evaluating newspaper stories that reproduce speeches, interviews, and reports — emphasizing accurate reproduction, treatment (condensing and unifying), and use of human-interest material where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — accurate reproduction of utterances
rubrics_metrics.description: To reproduce as accurately as possible the ideas expressed by a speaker, by a person interviewed, or by the author of a report is obviously the only object in writing a news story dealing with such material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story should aim to reflect the original ideas faithfully. Four common faults that endanger accuracy are carelessness in taking down what is said; playing up statements taken from their context so as to be misleading; unintentional distortion by giving disproportionate space or emphasis to some points; and misrepresentation because of political partisanship or other bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation fidelity (substance, form, and spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: All quotation, direct or indirect, should be accurate not only in substance and form but also in spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations must preserve the author's or speaker's intended meaning — not merely literal words. A verbatim phrase used as a lead or highlight must still reflect the actual thought or purpose of the original; otherwise it misleads readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid playing up statements out of context
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement taken verbatim from a speech, interview, or report, may be played up in the lead in such a way that it does not give the actual thought or purpose of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not isolate striking phrases and present them as representative if they were incidental. Leads and highlights should be chosen so they do not distort the overall meaning of the utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distortion by disproportionate emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: By confining his news story to only one or two phases of the subject discussed, a writer often gives an erroneous impression of the whole speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate space and emphasis so that the parts given prominence accurately reflect the relative importance of points made by the speaker or report; avoid selective emphasis that changes the perceived message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partisan suppression or distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Distortion and suppression of speeches, interviews, or reports because of political or other bias is indefensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and editors must not omit or alter material to fit partisan aims. Present material neutrally and fully enough to allow readers to judge; political or ideological editing that changes meaning is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment — condense, summarize, and combine coherently
rubrics_metrics.description: Since news stories of this class must consist largely of direct and indirect quotation from an utterance, the problem of presenting news of this kind is usually that of condensing, summarizing, and combining different parts of the available material into a unified, coherent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skill is required to select and compress material without losing sense or emphasis. The writer must merge disparate parts of a speech or report into a readable narrative that preserves meaning and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use description of speaker and circumstances to stimulate interest
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing up interviews and speeches the reporter has a chance to portray clearly and attractively the speaker and the circumstances, thus stimulating the reader's interest in the utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, add brief, vivid description of the speaker, the setting, or the audience to engage readers — but do so without allowing descriptive detail to overshadow accurate reporting of the ideas expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews — opportunity for human-interest and personality portrait
rubrics_metrics.description: In interviews, on the other hand, it is possible to bring out the human interest element in portraying the character and personality of the person interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interview material to reveal character and human interest while preserving the factual content of the subject's ideas. Signed interview pieces increasingly include reporter's questions to frame this portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of reporter's questions (suppress or include appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the purpose of an interview is to present the ideas of the person interviewed, the reporter's questions, which are a necessary means of obtaining an expression of these ideas, are suppressed in many stories. In other stories, the questions are embodied in the answers or are repeated by the person interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide case-by-case whether to suppress, paraphrase, or print questions verbatim. There is a growing tendency, particularly in signed stories of interviews, to give the reporter's questions — do so when they clarify context or add transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize genre similarities and differences (speech vs. report vs. interview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches, lectures, addresses, and sermons may be considered in the same class with interviews and reports, because all are alike in being some form of utterance. A speech and a report differ only in the fact that one is spoken and the other is written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat them similarly as reproductions of utterance (largely informative), but adapt technique: reports may allow for more textual condensation; interviews permit more personality detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary informative function (limited field for human interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: As reproductions of utterances, news stories of speeches and reports must be largely informative. Except for an occasional opportunity to describe the speaker or the audience, they offer practically no field for human interest development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep focus on transmitting ideas and facts. Avoid forcing human-interest angles where they don't exist; use descriptive material sparingly to support understanding and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When appropriate, follow a lead with verbatim report
rubrics_metrics.description: Note — Following the lead given below was a verbatim report of the speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some cases (e.g., important formal speeches) it is appropriate to use a lead summarizing significance and then present substantial verbatim passages or the full text as supplied by a stenographer, especially when exact wording is essential to meaning.
